name: Landmarks of the Ancient Kingdom of Saba, Marib
alternate_names: Landmarks of the Ancient Kingdom of Saba in Marib Governorate
coordinate_note: Converted from the central-point coordinates given in the State Party's nomination executive summary for the Ancient City of Ma'rib component (15°25'36.76"N, 45°20'6.82"E). UNESCO's property page states that georeferenced polygons will be published once UNESCO receives the GIS data, so no official single coordinate was read there. The inscribed property is a serial property of seven component parts spread across Marib Governorate; the nomination states that Sirwah lies 40 km west of Ma'rib and that the dam is about 8 km west of the ancient capital. This marker is a practical single-point reference for the ancient city only.
significance_summary: UNESCO describes the property as a serial property of seven archaeological sites in Marib Governorate, central Yemen, that bear witness to the Kingdom of Saba, dating from the 1st millennium BCE to the arrival of Islam around 630 CE. The components include the walled city of Ma'rib, the fortified city of Sirwah, temples at Awam and Bar'an, and the Ma'rib dam and irrigation system, which UNESCO describes as the largest ancient man-made oasis. UNESCO's news item says the sites reflect the Kingdom's centralised administration, its control of much of the incense route and its trade links with the Mediterranean and East Africa. It was inscribed in January 2023 under criteria (iii) and (iv) through the Committee's emergency procedure, and placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger at the same session.

threat_categories.evidence_summary: The Committee inscribed the property under the emergency procedure because of what UNESCO's news item calls threats of destruction from the ongoing conflict, and the 2023 decision links the property's threats to war and conflict. Conflict damage is documented in events[]: National Geographic and ICCROM reported in June 2015 that an airstrike on the night of 31 May 2015 damaged the northern sluice of the ancient dam (Yemeni officials attributed the strike to coalition forces; the Saudi embassy did not respond to a request for comment), a 2017 article by Khalidi states that Sirwah was bombarded in April and May 2015, and ICOMOS's 2022 evaluation cites an airstrike on the northern dam bank in 2015 and bombing at Sirwah in 2018 and describes some attributes as 'gravely damaged' by ongoing military attacks. For present conditions: the State Party's report to the 2024 Committee session says unstable conditions and armed conflict prevent local authorities from carrying out field inspections and projects, with the security situation at Sirwah a particular obstacle, while most sites in the Marib Oasis are in a better security situation; a State Party report listed by UNESCO under 2024 says the area is still not safe, particularly Sirwah and the Ma'rib dam. The Committee's 2026 decision again asks for a Reactive Monitoring mission 'once conditions allow'. Press reporting in August-September 2026 describes renewed fighting in Marib Governorate: Al Jazeera reported on 8 August 2026 that the Houthis had renewed shelling of Marib city, with two civilians killed and 14 wounded on the Friday according to Yemen's Health Ministry; on 10 September 2026 it reported pro-government forces and the Houthis attacking each other in Marib and al-Jawf; and Arab News on 19 September 2026 relayed government-side military sources describing clashes on fronts west and south of Marib city. Al Jazeera also reported attacks on Marib city on 16 August 2026 and Arab News reported army-claimed fighting south of Marib city on 20 September 2026. None of the five 2026 articles reviewed mentions the heritage components, and the sources reviewed do not establish the distance between these fighting locations and individual components, nor report new damage to the property in 2026.
threat_categories.date_note: Date of the airstrike reported to have damaged the northern sluice of the ancient dam (ICCROM, 3 June 2015); this is the earliest precisely dated conflict damage in the sources reviewed. Khalidi (2017) dates the bombardment of Sirwah to April and May 2015, and the conflict is ongoing.

threat_categories.evidence_summary: The Committee's 2023 inscription decision lists, among the property's threats, urban sprawl that has destroyed some areas with archaeological potential, demolition of post-Sabaean vernacular architecture, vandalism and looting, gravely damaged physical fabric and highly vulnerable integrity and authenticity, an unclear legal framework for the component parts and buffer zones, the absence of a management plan, funding gaps and the potential impacts of the 2018 Master Plan. The ICOMOS evaluation (approved 13 April 2022) describes the physical fabric as 'very poor', says the Ma'rib city walls have been quarried for building stone, that inscriptions at the Awam temple were pillaged, smuggled abroad and sold, that planned roads threaten the dam components, that 'Funds for protection and conservation of the component parts have not been available since 2015', that no state of conservation reports had been prepared since 2009, that only 'an estimated ten percent' of sites are excavated, and that monitoring relies mainly on satellite imagery, which ICOMOS considers inadequate. A State Party report listed by UNESCO under 2024 says no conservation projects had started at the sites and that donors are reluctant to fund projects in Yemen; the State Party's report to the 2024 session says increased damage is occurring because the property has no fences, that conflict damage, vandalism, looting and illegal activity are continuing concerns, that no encroachment has occurred within the boundaries since inscription, and that international assistance requests approved to date total zero. National Geographic (2022) reported that a 2,300-year-old inscribed alabaster statue base was ripped from the floor of the Awwam Temple and later appeared at a Paris auction house, and quoted Marib's antiquities director Sadeq al Salwi saying 'It's better that everything is under the ground. The sand is safety.' The Committee in 2024, 2025 and 2026 repeated the inscription-time requests (halt the 2018 Master Plan pending a Heritage Impact Assessment, restore funding, develop risk preparedness plans, include local tribes as custodians, extend protection to post-Sabaean vernacular architecture, complete an inventory, and notify the World Heritage Centre of major projects including fencing), and in 2025 and 2026 expressed concern at the lack of detailed, comprehensive information on the state of conservation. In 2026 it commended the State Party's recent efforts to preserve and monitor the property in a challenging context.
threat_categories.date_note: Chronic, multi-year concerns recorded by ICOMOS (2022) and the Committee (2023-2026); ICOMOS states conservation funding has been unavailable since 2015, but no single start date applies to the full set of concerns.

threat_categories.evidence_summary: The ICOMOS evaluation says sand is reburying parts of the Awam temple and the dam bank, and treats these environmental pressures as long-term issues rather than emergencies, though hard to address without funds. The nomination executive summary (State Party) cites torrential rains, flooding and desertification, and says agriculture relocates fertile sediments and damages archaeological remains. A State Party report listed by UNESCO under 2024 identifies rainwater, humidity, heat and drought as risks to be monitored. National Geographic (2022) captions describe sand slowly engulfing the pillars at Bar'an and reburying critical areas of the Awwam Temple; archaeologists quoted there say sand may help protect Bar'an from looters. This is a chronic, monitored pressure with mixed effects (sand both obscures and protects), not a documented acute event.
threat_categories.date_note: Chronic, long-term environmental pressures described in the 2022 ICOMOS evaluation and the State Party's nomination; no single start date applies.

threat_categories.evidence_summary: The ICOMOS evaluation states that flash floods have damaged a wall of the Bar'an temple, and the nomination states the area receives two rainy seasons per year and cites torrential rains and flooding as threats. The sources reviewed give no date for the Bar'an flood damage and do not document a specific recent flood event affecting the inscribed components. Reports of flooding at the modern Marib dam in 2020 were found but are not used, because the sources reviewed treat the modern dam and the ancient dam inconsistently. This category reflects documented exposure to flash flooding rather than a currently documented unrepaired disaster.
threat_categories.date_note: ICOMOS reports flash-flood damage to a wall of the Bar'an temple without giving a date; the exposure is long-standing.

status_history.decision_trigger: Critical Concern, applying the methodology top-down, and this is a close call with High Concern as the neighbouring status. Trigger matched: the site has been inaccessible to international monitoring and conservation bodies for an extended period for safety reasons, so its current condition cannot be verified. Evidence: ICOMOS could not carry out a technical evaluation mission in 2022 because of safety and security conditions; the Committee's 2023 inscription decision noted that a technical evaluation mission had not been possible, so authenticity, integrity, protection and management could not be fully assessed; the Committee asked the State Party to invite a Reactive Monitoring mission in 2023 and, in 2024, 2025 and 2026, welcomed or reiterated that the joint World Heritage Centre/ICOMOS mission take place 'once conditions allow', and it has not taken place on the evidence reviewed (more than three and a half years since inscription); and in 2025 and 2026 the Committee expressed concern at the lack of detailed, comprehensive information on the state of conservation. Counter-evidence weighed: national authorities report some field activity (the State Party's 2024 report says most sites in the Marib Oasis are in a better security situation and suitable for projects, and the Committee in 2026 commended the State Party's efforts to preserve and monitor the property), so the property is not wholly unmonitored; the inaccessibility is documented for international bodies and, in the State Party's own reports, for Sirwah and the dam. Other Critical triggers considered: (1) severe verified damage materially affecting the site now: the Committee's 2023 decision and ICOMOS's 2022 evaluation describe the fabric as gravely damaged or very poor, but no current damage assessment was available (the Committee itself asks for one), so this is not independently established as a present-tense finding; (2) active combat with fighting at or immediately adjacent to the site: Al Jazeera (8 August, 16 August and 10 September 2026) and Arab News (19 and 20 September 2026) report renewed shelling of Marib city and fighting on fronts in Marib Governorate, but none mentions the heritage components and the sources reviewed do not establish how close the fighting is to any component, so this trigger is treated as raising the weight of the first rather than as separately met; (3) collapse of protection or monitoring: not shown, since national management and UNESCO reporting continue. High Concern triggers also matched and would apply if Critical were not accepted: inscription on the List of World Heritage in Danger (since 2023, retained in 2024, 2025 and 2026) for substantive reasons; a region under active armed conflict with credible reporting on risk to cultural property; and significant historical damage whose repair has not begun (the State Party reports no conservation projects had started). A reviewer could reasonably call this High Concern if they weigh the national authorities' continuing on-site activity and the absence of any documented new damage to the components since 2018 more heavily than the long-pending international mission.
status_history.rationale: Historical damage is documented in the site's record, but the current classification is based on present conditions and the most recent credible evidence. The 2015 and 2018 attacks are recorded in events[] and are not themselves the basis for the present status. The present picture is of a World Heritage property that has been on the List of World Heritage in Danger since its inscription in January 2023, where the Committee has repeatedly asked for a monitoring mission that has not been possible, where the Committee said in 2025 and 2026 it lacks detailed, comprehensive information about the property's condition, where ICOMOS and the State Party report very poor fabric, looting, quarrying and no available conservation funding, and where renewed fighting in Marib Governorate was reported in August and September 2026 (the most recent article read is dated 20 September 2026). Against that, the evidence also shows that national authorities continue to monitor and report, that the State Party reports no encroachment within the boundaries since inscription, that the Committee in 2026 commended the State Party's efforts, that the State Party has reported most Marib Oasis sites to be in a better security situation, and that none of the five 2026 conflict reports reviewed mentions damage to the heritage components. The call therefore rests mainly on the unverifiable current condition and sustained lack of access for international monitoring, in a setting of renewed nearby fighting, rather than on documented new destruction. Confidence is Supported rather than Confirmed: the inaccessibility and the Committee's statements are drawn from UNESCO decisions and reports, but the 2025 and 2026 state of conservation reports could not be read, the 2026 conflict reporting is from news outlets and partly from government-side military sources, the location of fighting relative to the components is not established, and the security situation is changing. Confidence does not alter the status.

digital_preservation.coverage_note: Two of five categories have publicly findable evidence (photographic and academic/scholarly), which gives the moderate tier by the rubric (two to three categories). Coverage is thin: the UNESCO photo gallery holds only ten images and the Smithsonian page offers a small selection of historic excavation photographs. Archival records are marked false: UNESCO's documents page hosts the nomination dossier, ICOMOS evaluation and state of conservation material, but these are UNESCO process documents rather than a digitised archive of the site, and no dedicated digitised archive (for example excavation records) was located. No publicly viewable 3D model was verified: a 2007 peer-reviewed paper describes a photogrammetry and laser-scanning model of the northern sluice of the ancient dam made in January 2006, and the Smithsonian page says an international excavation team at the Awam Temple produced digital topographic plans and 3D models, but neither source indicates the models are publicly viewable, so 3D documentation is marked false rather than assumed. No virtual tour or 360-degree presentation was found. ICOMOS (2022) notes that most sites are unexcavated or only slightly excavated ('an estimated ten percent'), which limits what has been documented. The Madain Project page, a volunteer-run, ad-supported site, was opened but not counted because it is not an authoritative source. A reviewer may wish to re-check for DAI or other excavation archives that were not located in this pass.

evidence.description: UNESCO's World Heritage Centre hosts a public photo gallery for the property with 10 images, credited to Ebrahim Abdallah (4), Amr Alsrori (3), Irmgard Wagner (2) and the Deutsches Archaeologisches Institut (1).
The Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art online exhibition page on the Awam Temple includes a small gallery of historic photographs of the Wendell Phillips-era and later excavations at Marib.

Peer-reviewed article by Thomas Kersten (International Journal of Architectural Computing, 2007) on a virtual reality model of the northern sluice of the ancient dam made by combining photogrammetry and terrestrial laser scanning during January 2006 excavations, a collaboration between the German Archaeological Institute and HafenCity University Hamburg. The record read does not indicate that the model itself is publicly viewable.

events.title: Reports of bombardment and damage at Sirwah
events.description: A 2017 article by Lamya Khalidi in the International Journal of Middle East Studies states that the archaeological site of Sirwah was bombarded by the Saudi-led coalition in April and May 2015. National Geographic reported on 3 June 2015 that Yemeni sources told Iris Gerlach, director of the German Archaeological Institute's Sanaa Branch, that Sirwah had sustained considerable damage in recent fighting because of its proximity to the local governor's palace, and noted that communication shutdowns made independent confirmation difficult. Sirwah is now a component of the inscribed property.

events.title: Airstrike damages the northern sluice of the ancient Marib dam
events.description: ICCROM reported that an airstrike on the night of 31 May 2015 damaged the Great Dam of Marib, that ancient Sabaean inscriptions on the dam walls may have been affected, and that UNESCO Director-General Irina Bokova condemned the airstrikes. National Geographic reported that Gerlach relayed reports from sources close to local Marib leadership that the strike hit the better-preserved northern sluice, with images showing damage to its tower about 7 metres (23 feet) high; Yemeni officials said coalition forces were responsible, and the Saudi embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment. A 2022 National Geographic feature by Iona Craig describes the strike as having hit a sluice gate and torn through the remaining tower, leaving a pile of rubble. ICOMOS's 2022 evaluation also cites an airstrike on the northern dam bank in 2015.

events.title: Bombing at Sirwah cited by ICOMOS
events.description: ICOMOS's 2022 evaluation cites bombing at Sirwah in 2018 among the deliberate or conflict-related damage to components. The date is given by year only in the evaluation as read, and the same evaluation reports Sirwah as occupied by militia at the time, leaving its management unclear.

events.title: Associated Press reports Awwam Temple neglected in a front-line area
events.description: An Associated Press report described the Awwam Temple in Marib, which it called a front-line area in the Saudi-led war against Houthi rebels, as left neglected and unprotected. The report does not describe specific damage to the temple. Unnamed experts feared it remained at risk, and Anna Paolini, director of UNESCO's regional office in Qatar, was quoted saying 'it's sad to see what's happening'.

events.title: ICOMOS approves evaluation of the emergency nomination
events.description: ICOMOS approved its evaluation of the nomination on 13 April 2022; the State Party had submitted the nomination under the emergency procedure on 11 February 2022. ICOMOS could not carry out a technical evaluation mission because of safety and security conditions. It described the fabric as 'very poor', reported quarrying, pillaging and flash-flood damage, said conservation funding had not been available since 2015, and recommended inscription on an emergency basis under criteria (iii) and (iv) together with inscription on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

events.title: National Geographic feature reports looting, sand reburial and proximity of the front line
events.description: Iona Craig's National Geographic feature (September 2022 issue, published online 4 August 2022) reported that sand has reburied critical areas of the Awwam Temple, that a 2,300-year-old inscribed alabaster statue base was ripped from the floor and later appeared at a Paris auction house, and that a Houthi offensive had brought Marib city within range of rebel missiles. It quoted Sadeq al Salwi, Marib director of the General Organization of Antiquities and Museums: 'It's better that everything is under the ground. The sand is safety.'

events.title: Property inscribed on the World Heritage List and the List of World Heritage in Danger
events.description: At its 18th extraordinary session (listed by UNESCO as 24-25 January 2023; UNESCO's news item is dated 25 January 2023) the Committee inscribed the property under the emergency procedure, under criteria (iii) and (iv), and placed it on the List of World Heritage in Danger. UNESCO's news item gives threats of destruction from the ongoing conflict as the reason for the emergency procedure. The decision (18 EXT.COM 5.3) noted that a technical evaluation mission had not been possible, changed the property's name to 'Landmarks of the Ancient Kingdom of Saba, Marib', and set out nine numbered recommendations (the Committee's later decisions reiterate, among them, halting the 2018 Master Plan pending a Heritage Impact Assessment) and asked the State Party to invite a Reactive Monitoring mission.

events.title: State Party submits state of conservation report
events.description: UNESCO records that the State Party submitted its report on 19 February 2024. It reports that unstable conditions and armed conflict prevent local authorities from carrying out field inspections and projects, with Sirwah a particular obstacle, while most sites in the Marib Oasis are in a better security situation and suitable for projects; that increased damage is occurring because the property has no fences; that no encroachment has occurred within the boundaries since inscription; and that funding, training and skilled personnel are lacking, with zero international assistance requests approved to date.

events.title: World Heritage Committee decision 46 COM 7A.34 on Marib
events.description: The Committee welcomed the State Party's informative report on damage and challenges, requested implementation of the inscription-time recommendations, encouraged detailed damage documentation when conditions allow, said urgent stabilisation should be limited to cases where collapse or further damage is imminent, welcomed the invitation of a joint World Heritage Centre/ICOMOS Reactive Monitoring mission once conditions allow, called for international support including through the UNESCO Heritage Emergency Fund, retained the property on the List of World Heritage in Danger and asked for an updated report by 1 February 2025.

events.title: World Heritage Committee decision 47 COM 7A.55 on Marib
events.description: The Committee expressed concern about the lack of detailed, comprehensive information on the property's state of conservation, reiterated the inscription-time requests, again called for a joint Reactive Monitoring mission once conditions allow (to advise on a Desired state of conservation for removal from the Danger List), appealed for cooperation against illicit trafficking of cultural property from Yemen, retained the property on the Danger List and asked for an updated report by 1 February 2026.

events.title: World Heritage Committee decision 48 COM 7A.20 on Marib
events.description: At its 48th session (Busan) the Committee commended the State Party's recent efforts to preserve and monitor the property in a challenging context, again expressed concern about the lack of detailed, comprehensive information on its state of conservation, reiterated its earlier requests, again called for a Reactive Monitoring mission once conditions allow, retained the property on the List of World Heritage in Danger, and asked for an updated report by 1 February 2027 for the 49th session. The month of the decision was not confirmed in this pass.

events.title: Renewed shelling of Marib city reported
events.description: Al Jazeera reported on 8 August 2026 that government forces launched attacks on Houthi positions hours after the Houthis renewed shelling of Marib city. It reported that on the Friday an attack on Marib killed two civilians and wounded 14, according to Yemen's Health Ministry, and that the Houthis said they targeted a military camp on the city's outskirts; Deputy Information Minister Mohammed Gezan said the Houthis had resumed shelling civilian neighbourhoods. The article does not mention any heritage site.

events.title: Further attacks on Marib city reported
events.description: Al Jazeera reported on 16 August 2026 that the Houthis launched missile and drone strikes on Marib city (on the Saturday evening, 15 August) and al-Makha (on the Sunday). Marib's government media office said six ballistic missiles and four drones hit residential neighbourhoods, wounding four people, and the Yemeni military said it carried out 181 operations against Houthi positions across several governorates over the weekend. These are the accounts of the parties named in the article; it does not mention any heritage site.

events.title: Fighting reported on fronts in Marib Governorate
events.description: Al Jazeera reported on 10 September 2026 that, over recent weeks, pro-government forces had attacked Houthi-held areas in Marib and al-Jawf and the Houthis had retaliated, and cited aid agencies as saying at least 194 people were killed and 880 wounded in two weeks of fighting across Taiz, the western coast, al-Jawf, Marib and Dhalea (a total for several governorates, not Marib alone). Arab News reported on 19 September 2026, citing unnamed government-side military sources, that government forces advanced on the Al-Mashjah front west of Marib city and that airstrikes reportedly hit Houthi forces on southern fronts; the report carried no Houthi response or independent verification. Neither article mentions the heritage components. Arab News reported on 20 September 2026 that the Yemeni army's military media director said more than 80 Houthi fighters were killed in 24 hours of fighting at Hareb, Mala'a and Um Raish, south of Marib city; the article presents these as the army's unverified claims and does not mention heritage components.

changelog.change: Revision of the 2026-10-12 draft for the 2026-10-14 reference date. (1) Re-read Decision 48 COM 7A.20 (whc.unesco.org/en/decisions/9011): session Busan 2026; commends State Party; concern at lack of detailed information; reiterates eight inscription-time recommendations; reiterates Reactive Monitoring mission request once conditions allow; retains the property on the Danger List; updated report due 1 February 2027. (2) Corrected DPI: archival_records changed from true to false because UNESCO's documents page hosts nomination/ICOMOS/state of conservation process documents, not a digitised archive of the site; DPI now photographic + academic_scholarly = 2 categories, still the moderate tier. (3) Added two 2026 news sources (Al Jazeera 16 August; Arab News 20 September) and one event; neither mentions heritage components. (4) Known gap: UNESCO's property page (list/1700) could not be re-fetched on 2026-10-14 (fetch tool refused the URL); current Danger List status rests on the 2026 decision text, which retains the property on the List, plus the 2026-10-12 read of the property page. Status call unchanged: Critical Concern / Supported, close call with High Concern. | Independent verification pass 2026-10-14: (1) corrected mission wording in decision_trigger (2023 decision asked the State Party to invite a mission; 'once conditions allow' is the wording of 2024-2026); (2) 2023 event: recommendations/mission wording aligned to decision page; (3) 2024 decision: stabilisation limit now 'collapse or further damage is imminent'; (4) 16 Aug 2026 Al Jazeera event: timing of Marib strikes (Saturday evening) and 181 operations 'across several governorates'.
